job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Sam Wagner

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thank you for talking with me. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm up at six and drive twenty minutes to a car-parts plant outside Ulm. I'm a junior test engineer, so I run brake components on a test rig, log the numbers and write up why one failed. I finished mechanical engineering at Aalen in the summer, and I started here in the autumn.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like being on the shop floor, with the noise and the smell of oil, and I like the old foreman Herr Brandt, who teaches me tricks the textbooks skip. What wears me out is the paperwork after every test. I rent a room in a shared flat with a friend from university, Lukas, and my parents live an hour away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, nothing special then. At work I'd carry on as I am and tell my mates it's the same noise as every other tech wave. I trust a brake test I ran myself more than a report some program wrote.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm calm. Test engineering is part hands-on and part paperwork, and the paperwork is the only bit software might touch. My pay is decent, I have no debt and a good chunk saved, and my parents would help if needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going: finish my probation, learn the rig properly and do the paperwork faster. I'd put 300 euros a month aside and start looking at a small flat of my own in two years. Nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It feels like when a long road gets resurfaced and still goes to the same place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you never use AI tools. Why not?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I tried a chatbot once and it made up a standard that doesn't exist. After that I decided I'd rather do it by hand until somebody shows me it's reliable. That's not fear, it's just caution.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would worry you, if anything, even if nothing changed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car industry in this region is shaky because of electric cars, and the plant I work for makes parts for combustion engines. That's the real risk, honestly, more than AI. If the orders drop, we'd feel it first.

I'd carry on and tell friends nothing really changes.
think: I'm **calm**, because the hands-on part of testing is safe and the paperwork is small.
My real risk is the plant's **orders**, since it makes combustion-engine parts.
do: Finish my **probation** and learn the test rig properly.
Put **300 euros** a month aside toward a small flat.
feel: **Calm**, like a resurfaced road that goes to the same place.

fieldNote: His resistance is about **reliability**: a chatbot once invented a standard.

steps.text: Finish the probation period and learn the brake test rig properly
Put 300 euros a month toward a flat deposit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's coming, and the paperwork side of my job will shrink. At work I'd want clear rules on who is responsible for a test report. If software writes the test report, my signature is still on it, and I won't sign what I haven't checked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'm a bit uneasy. The rig work is mine, but half my week is writing up results, and I could see one engineer doing that for ten people. I don't think I'd be first to go, because I'm on the floor, but plants can shrink.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the reporting software the plant brings in, but only as much as needed. I'd ask Herr Brandt to teach me the repair and calibration jobs, since those are hands-on. I'd save 400 euros a month and not take on any loans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's the feeling of knowing a change is coming but not seeing yet where it lands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part of your day could software take over first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The write-ups and the data tables, which take about half my week. A machine could do them in minutes. The part it can't do is knowing that a strange noise means a worn bearing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if your boss asked everyone to use it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use it, grumbling. I'm slow with new software, but I'm not stupid. I'd ask for a training day and a person I can ask questions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast, and I'd say that to anyone who'd listen. At work people would ask me, as a young engineer, and I'd say I don't know. Nobody I work with can tell me what my job looks like in two years, and that's the scary part.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm anxious. The thinking side of my job, the test planning and the reports, could be gone in a couple of years. The hands-on rig work lasts about three years longer, but the plant might not need as many of us. I'd expect cuts, and I'm one of the newest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save everything I can, around 700 euros a month, and cut out holidays and the car upgrade I wanted. I'd ask Herr Brandt about a technician's path, where hands-on skills matter. I'd also keep my head down at work and not make noise, and talk to my parents about moving home if things go badly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd feel like I was standing at the edge of a platform, waiting for a train I can't see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only two years, which decision would you make first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start by cancelling the holiday I'd planned and putting that money in the bank. Then I'd ask for a longer contract, if the plant would give it. It's not a dramatic plan, but I'm not a dramatic person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them over Sunday lunch that I'm okay but nervous. My father worked thirty years at a machine shop and he'd say hands are always needed. He might be right for a bit, but I'd keep it as a maybe.

I'd tell colleagues honestly that I **don't know**.
think: I'm **anxious**, because the test planning and reports could be gone in two years.

His plan is cautious and low-drama, in line with his resistance to risk.

steps.text: Save 700 euros a month and cancel the planned holiday

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a bit of breathing room, but it's still fast. At work I'd keep doing my job well, because the best protection I know is being useful on the floor. I'd rather be the engineer who's always there and always knows the rig than the one with the fancy slides.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm uneasy more than anxious. I'd expect the reporting to be automated by then and the plant to need fewer people on the engineering side. But a test engineer who also understands machines is harder to replace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd take a part-time course in mechatronics, since that mixes machines and software, and I'd get over my dislike of new tools by trying them on small things. I'd save 500 euros a month and keep my flat share. In two years I'd decide whether to stay in cars or move to energy or rail.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I can breathe. Five years feels like I can't ignore it, but I'm not drowning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the three extra years before robots reach hands-on work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop putting off learning the software side. I'd rather learn it while no one is forcing me. I'd also be honest that I'm slow with new tech, so I'd start early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you stop doing, if you had five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look at trains and wind turbines. Those need people who can fix machines, and I like machines more than screens. It's a pragmatic bet, not a dream.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty and I'd just keep going. At work I'd tell colleagues to learn something new every year, and I'd say it to myself too. Ten years is long enough to learn a trade twice, so I'm not going to lose sleep tonight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm not worried much. By 2036 I'd be 32, and I could have moved into design, maintenance management or a small firm of my own. Robots arrive for hands-on work three years after, and I'd be at the top of my area by then. The real unknown is the car industry, not the AGI date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my job, buy a small flat in a few years and take courses slowly, one a year. I'd try the software tools when the plant has them, and I'd still prefer paper for my own notes. I'd also look at the next generation of rigs, which will be semi-automatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm. A decade is enough to turn around even if I'm slow to start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, would you plan differently?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start thinking about family around thirty, and I'd want a place near my parents. The date doesn't change that much. A secure job in a town I like is what matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about family and home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I'm honest, I'd probably wait and see. Ten years lets me wait and watch what the others do, and I'm good at that. It's a weakness and a strength.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. I could handle slow change on my own terms, but two years takes the choosing away from me. What would help is a plant that tells staff early what's changing, paid training days, and a clear path for people who work with their hands.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that I'm not afraid of machines, I work with them all day. I only want somebody to explain what's coming in plain words. Herr Brandt says the same, and he's sixty-two.

headlineQuote: I could handle slow change on my own terms, but two years takes the choosing away from me.
portrait: Sam is **22**, a mechanical engineering graduate working as a junior test engineer at a car-parts plant near Ulm.
He has no debt and good savings, shares a flat with a university friend, and his parents live an hour away.
He is centre and pragmatic, blames **no one** in particular, but fears the plant's shaky combustion-engine orders more than AI.
He is resistant: he avoids AI tools, prefers the familiar and plans to **wait and see** while he builds hands-on skills.
biggestWorry: AI by **2028** worries him most, because two years takes away his chance to choose the pace.
whatWouldHelp: Early, plain **warnings** from his plant, paid training days and a clear path for hands-on workers.
